Thermal stability of a recombinant lipase from Bacillus sp. strain K4
Abstract
We expressed the lipase gene of Bacillus sp. strain K4 in Escherichia coli and measured how temperature, pH and two point mutations change the activity and the stability of the purified enzyme. The wild-type enzyme had its highest activity at 55 °C and pH 8.0, and the double mutant kept 74 % of its initial activity after one hour at 60 °C, compared with 31 % for the wild type. Activity towards PNPB was measured in every experiment.
Introduction
Lipases play a pivotal part in the hydrolysis of triglycerides at the oil and water interface of emulsions. Enzymes from thermophilic soil bacteria are used in detergents and in the synthesis of esters, where reactions run above 50 °C. Studies show that lipases from soil isolates tolerate organic solvents better than those from mesophilic hosts. The lid domain covers the active site in water and opens at the interface (Smith, 2020; Okafor and Lindqvist, 2021). Earlier work on a related strain reported a disulfide bridge near the lid (Moreno et al., 2018), but the effect of that bridge on stability was not tested.
Materials and methods
The gene was amplified from genomic DNA and cloned into pET-28a. Cells were grown in LB medium at 37 °C to an optical density of 0.6 and induced with 0.5 mM IPTG for 16 h at 20 °C. Cells were harvested by centrifugation and lysed by sonication. The lysate was centrifuged at 15,000 g for 30 min in order to remove the cell debris, and the supernatant was loaded on a nickel affinity column. The end result of the purification was a single band of 32 kDa on the gel.
Activity was measured with p-nitrophenyl butyrate (PNPB) as the substrate in 50 mM Tris-HCl buffer. The release of p-nitrophenol was followed at 410 nm for 5 min. One unit was defined as the amount of enzyme that releases 1 µmol of p-nitrophenol per minute. The mutants C87S and A112C were made by overlap extension PCR, and the sequence of each construct was confirmed.
For the stability assays the enzyme was incubated at 50, 60 and 70 °C, and samples were taken every 10 min. The residual activity was measured at 37 °C. Half-lives were obtained from a first-order fit of the residual activity against time.
Results
Activity rose steadily up to 55 °C, highlighting the thermophilic origin of the strain. Above this temperature the activity fell, and at 70 °C it was below 10 % of the maximum. The pH profile had a single peak at pH 8.0.
The wild-type enzyme had a half-life of 42 min at 60 °C. The single mutant A112C, which can form a second disulfide bridge, had a half-life of 96 min, and the double mutant reached 118 min. The gain of the double mutant over the wild type was significant (p < 0.01). The mutation did not merely shift the optimum temperature but also widened the range of stable pH values. It is worth noting that the enzyme retained activity after three freeze and thaw cycles.
The kinetic constants did not change much between the variants: the Km for PNPB was 0.21 mM for the wild type and 0.24 mM for the double mutant, as shown in Fig. 7 of the supplement. The catalytic rate of the double mutant was 12.5 % lower than that of the wild type.
Discussion
These data suggest that the second disulfide bridge may stabilise the lid domain in its closed form. A rigid lid would explain why the gain in stability comes with a small loss of rate. The ​thermal unfolding of the lid was not measured directly — circular dichroism of the isolated domain would answer this — and the crystal structure of the mutant is still missing — a model was used instead — so the position of the new bridge is predicted and not observed.
A similar trade-off was described for a lipase from a hot spring isolate (Okafor and Lindqvist, 2021). The double mutant is a candidate for use in detergents that are applied at 60 °C, ‮where the wild type loses most of its activity within an hour.
Here is the revised paragraph with the corrected values: the yield of purified enzyme was 4.2 mg per litre of culture.
